utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I remind the admiral of the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, can you please tell me, what can be the basis for a commander in the middle of operations to make the so-called corrective decisions?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If a commander establishes that the factual situation in terms of carrying out orders in its combat activities is such that it requires a change in the previous decisions, regardless of whether on account of casualties or because the enemy unexpectedly and suddenly launched certain operations or stepped up firing, there are a number of different possibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can this occur also pursuant to a proposal by one of the subordinates?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's a possibility. This is often the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about Bosanka and Strincjera, the forts that were attacked between the 9th and 13th of November? Were those features within the zone of responsibility of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You were the commander who was best placed to assess the situation in the zone of responsibility, weren't you, and to make requests or express the need for the attack to go on for a longer time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean by go on for a longer time, or prolong the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If the previous attack fails to attain the objectives or if one objective was attained but another objective emerged and had to be accomplished, speaking strictly in terms of the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. Every day, the command of the 2nd operational group pursuant to a proposal by a subordinate command, or on its own, on its own accord, makes decisions as to how to use its subordinate forces. Therefore, the commander, specifically myself, would not make such a decision on my own to continue the attack because the objective of the previous order was not reached. But again, pursuant to a decision of the command of the 2nd Operational Group and my own proposal, the attack could be continued, as was the case here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The command of the 2nd Operational Group, the proposal to continue operations, for example, in the Mostar area, would this proposal be given to it by the commander of the 37th Corps, in view of the fact that he would be the person best placed to assess the situation in that particular territory because it lies within his zone of responsibility, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And he was the one who made proposals on how to use his forces. And the command of the 2nd Operational Group would then adopt or fail to adopt or approve this proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Would the situation be the same with the 2nd Corps in relation to the 2nd Operational Group then?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I believe there is no difference there. The only difference being that the area of combat operations along the ridge between Dubrava and Srdj was so close to Trebinje and the command of the 2nd Operational Group that the influence could even have been more immediate.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But what I'm aiming at is to establish a principle. Is this the principle according to which the subordinate units and their superior command operate?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right. This was the principle according to which decisions were made.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Among other things, the reason was the enormous territory to be covered, the commander of the 2nd OG could not be present in each and every sector of this territory during a single day, could he?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's quite correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you give the OTP an interview between the 1st and 5th of July 2002, the 6th and the 12th of September 2003, in February 2004, on the 12th and 13th of March 2004, and between the 15th and 18th of March 2004?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On that occasion, did you tell the truth to the investigators who were questioning or interviewing you?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I will show you a portion of your statement on page 51, in the English version, pages 55 and 56, the interview that took place between the 6th and 12th of September.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if an interview is going to be cited to the witness, we would ask that the pages in his language be presented to him. The physical page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, all these interviews are quite comprehensive in terms of the number of pages they comprise. I don't have the sufficient number of copies. I can quote from the interviews, and my learned friend and colleague is surely in possession of these interviews. Should I make a mistake, she is always free to step in and correct me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you have a copy that can be given to the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Unfortunately not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Often very difficult for the witness to follow simply hearing a reading of it. It may be necessary to show him a copy from time to time.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to half of these issues, Your Honour, as you must be aware, the transcript was never made. And we have faced situations where we had to show other witnesses what they said in their interviews; and yet, we've never faced a situation where we had to place their statements in front of them during their testimony because that was never requested.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Carry on for the moment, Mr. Rodic. We will see how it works out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, the question asked by the investigator was the following. He says "and we shall conclude now for today. Can you tell us who made the decision to relaunch the offensive?" Your answer was: "Well, General Strugar. I received an order to take Bosanka, or rather he asked that a proposal be drawn up on how to use the forces, I believe."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour. I'm not able to find in the English version pages that Mr. Rodic mentioned -- the passage. Perhaps if he has it, he can put it on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page in English would be 56.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If perhaps the ERN were on it would be more helpful than the page number because there are different page numbers here.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What has been disclosed to us are the pages that I'm giving you in the English copy. In addition to the ERN number, there are also the regular page numbers starting with 1, and this is page 56.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What you said in the interview, is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that clearly. It's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you point out that the situation in relation to the operations being carried out by your units in November 1991 was important in relation to Bosanka and that Srdj was not to be taken?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. What I pointed out, if you want, it's right there in the continuation of this section or the following section, why there was a proposal to take Bosanka. That's what the investigator wanted to know specifically. Why after Zarkovica we set out for Bosanka.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please explain, if you can. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told him that between Brgat, where the command was of the mixed detachment of the TO, and later the command of the 3rd Battalion, and Zarkovica, there is a road, the only road in the area which was used for transporting supplies. And also, that we at Bosanka were often under heavy fire, and we were suffering losses, especially after the Bosanka fort was reinforced following the arrival of volunteers on the convoy that sailed into Dubrovnik on the 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are we talking about the convoy under the leadership of Stjepan Mesic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the one. That's what our proposal to the command was, to take Bosanka, and this proposal was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In the July 2002 interview, did you tell the investigators that there was never an order to take Srdj?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Would you cite, please, the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The page is, the English page is 66 and 67.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, in essence, I answered hundreds of questions in all these interviews, and there are no discrepancies. A possible exception might be constituted by the fact that my first interview in July was given before I had a chance to go through the entire military files as they relate to the Dubrovnik operation. However, these minor corrections to my answers cast no doubt in any essential way on any of my answers that may or may not be slightly different, nor do they cast a doubt on my sincerity and truthfulness. As far as Srdj is concerned, I'll say it again. When I said that Srdj was never a target for us, I was speaking about myself, I was speaking about my command. It was never my aim to take Srdj. I had no such aim to carry out. But I don't think it was either in relation to the command of the 2nd Operational Group or the General Staff. I never said anything about them. The last time around you simply didn't allow me to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If you could just provide a brief explanation because there's still plenty for us to go through today.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well. I found a directive that you failed to present this time. There's another directive nine pages long issued by the General Staff. And what it says there is "take Srdj." During the war, however, I never heard of it. I never saw this directive. It was only after we were allowed to gain access to the files that I found this one. And that's when it became clearer to me why the command of the 2nd Operational Group had ordered those forts to be taken, including Srdj. I've finished my explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, now, from October 2001 to August 2003, you prepared your Defence case. You studied the documents of the Prosecution, and you gathered together material evidence and had conversations with potential witnesses in your Defence. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, including my Defence team and the investigators. I wasn't able to talk to potential witnesses myself, but with some of them, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind the fact that at the beginning, before the Tribunal and via the information media in Serbia, as we were able to see, with the situation with the Nin magazine, you denied your guilt with respect to the indictment concerning Dubrovnik in 1991, can you tell us now please why you changed your position and pleaded guilty? What led you to do that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not confess to begin with because the indictment was such -- on such a broad scale and so incorrect that it did not actually refer to me in a large number -- a large portion of its contents. For example, criminal enterprise did not refer to me because had Admiral Djurovic not been killed, I would never have found myself in Dubrovnik in the first place or here in The Hague either. So that was just pure coincidence that I came to take up his command. Second, I do not feel responsible or guilty for all the destruction of the settlements and neighbourhoods that are mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, let's not go that far afield. We've already --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. A question is on the floor. The witness has attempted to answer it. It doesn't suit Defence counsel, but it's his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You may take it up further in re-examination, if you wish, Ms. Somers. He has given the answer, and we'll take it from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, when I asked you that question, I wasn't asking you about parts of the indictment that were dropped, but the events linked to the 6th of December that you confessed to, was that in the first indictment? Were they contained in the first indictment, the original one?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That portion was in the original indictment, and I accepted the command responsibility for the 6th of December. And what -- the fact that I didn't manage to stop the attack, the willful attack on the part of the command of the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you do so? When it came to the 6th of December, why didn't you do so immediately if you considered yourself to be responsible?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. When do you mean "straight away," "immediately"?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When you pleaded on the first occasion in November 2001. You entered your plea.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The points weren't set out in that way. They weren't formulated in that way, in aiding and abetting and so on and so forth. Count was not formulated in that way in the indictment. I was asked about the entire indictment to begin with, and then the individual counts of the indictment. And I wasn't responsible pursuant to those counts or to blame at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In that original indictment, were there counts referring to the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But they were not formulated. That particular count was not formulated and worded in such a way that I should be held responsible for command responsibility, and that was in order as regards Article 7(3), and for failure to react. Or rather, I wasn't able to stop that willful attack. That was not how the count of the indictment was formulated, and that's what I wanted to say. That's not how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we now go into private session for the next portion of my cross-examination because we're going to discuss the agreement that the witness made with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Private session, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, can you tell me, please, on the 5th of December in Cavtat, when roughly speaking did you conclude your talks with Minister Rudolf?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We concluded our talks at around 12.00, a little after 12.00. And then we had lunch after that, which would make it around 1.00. Half past 1.00 at the latest when I left Cavtat.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, where you went after you left Cavtat on that particular day.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I went to Trebinje, to the command post, 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Trebinje at the command post of the 2nd OG?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps half an hour. I can't be sure. Half an hour to one hour. But anyway, I went back to Kupari, and I was there at around 5.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And what were you doing in Kupari when you got there from Trebinje?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in my command with the staff of the command, and I informed them of the concluded negotiations. I conveyed this to my immediate associates and said that all the units must be informed that the agreement had been reached and that there would be a cease-fire imminent, and that that news should reach each and every unit. I also said that in addition to the fact that the agreement would be signed the next day officially, that the cease-fire and the agreement came into effect at 12.00 and that the units should be told that from the morning it was forbidden to open fire. And that this should be relayed to the units by telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, who you reported this to and further down the line who passed this information on to the subordinate units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said my immediate staff, that is to say, the chief of staff, the chief of the operational department, Colonel Kovacevic, my immediate associates and people who were directly responsible for the operation in terms of reporting.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did they pass on that information to the subordinate units, the order, in fact, the order on a cease-fire effective on the 6th of December, and that on the 6th of December at 12.00 noon there should be an absolute observance of the cease-fire?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That's just how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, please, who specifically performed that task.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the commander has to say which telephone he is using and issue assignments. It is my duty to order -- to let the chief of staff know about this order, and then he goes down the line. Now, if you want the exact procedure, I can, of course, tell you. But whether those were the steps, I can't say. The chief of the operational department conveys the information to the duty officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you receive feedback information? That's what I'm interested in. Who from your staff informed the subordinate units on the 5th of December that a cease-fire had been agreed upon and was to come into force? Because I assume this was important information. You, as the commander, did you have any feedback information? And if so, who carried the task out?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't ask for feedback information, nor did I need it. I was just informed that the order had been carried out and that the message had been conveyed to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Who informed you about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The duty -- or rather, the head of the operational department who was at the command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And who was on duty that day? Who was the duty officer at the forward command post of Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was Frigate Captain Slobodan Kozaric.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So that means he reported back to you that your orders had been carried out?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely correct. I was perhaps at the command post while this was actually being done because I stayed there perhaps longer than half an hour. Maybe an hour. So I might have been there while that was being carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, this order of yours, was it conveyed orally down to the subordinate units, or was this conveyed in written form? How was this generally done? How was this done on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All orders, important ones, which are passed down the subordinate units via their commands, if they are not written out in document form, are recorded in the war logbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now, in the logbook, war logbook, of the 9th VPS, was this entry recorded about having conveyed subordinate units individually about the cease-fire that was to come into force on the 6th of December? Was that done and recorded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it quite certainly wasn't written down as an individual order or the individual units concerned. Most probably, it says, and that is usually the case, that all subordinate units or commands were informed thereof. Now, if we were to go on to enumerate all these, then you would have 20 or 30 units and commands that would have to be listed for that one order.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, just tell me if you know, apart from that war logbook whether there was any other written trace or document with an entry of that kind? That is to say, information to units about the cease-fire on the 6th of December, if you can tell me. If not, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. Perhaps in addition to the war logbook, there is a book where all sorts of things are written, a sort of scrapbook. That's the unofficial word they use at the operations duty centre. Perhaps it is within the operations scrapbook.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And as you were preparing your Defence, did you have insight into this war logbook? Did you see it written there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did have insight. Yes. If you're interested in whether this was conveyed for the commander of the 3rd Battalion, I know it was, and everybody knows it was. He knows that, too. That's not in dispute at all. If that's the point of your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: No, the point of my question is exactly what I asked you. As for the commander of the 3rd Battalion, I would have asked you directly. Tell me, when did you leave Kupari and where did you go to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know exactly, of course, after all these years. But I think I finished between 5.00 and 6.00, and I went straight to Kumbor because I had things to do at the command. I had a lot of work as a matter of fact, especially with regard to the evacuation of different units. But it was the 5th sector of Pula that had its turn then.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, the command of the 9th VPS, on the 5th of December, in its regular combat report, did it inform its superior command that during the course of the day an important meeting had been held in Cavtat and what was agreed upon at that meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is normal procedure. But I personally went to the commander, General Strugar, and I informed him in detail about all the points of the agreement. I think that that's for sure. And as for that report, it is probably contained there. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the usher now to distribute this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, is this a regular combat report of your command dated the 5th of December 1991 addressed to the 2nd Operational Group, signed by the chief of staff?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In this document, is there any mention whatsoever in a single word of your meeting with Minister Rudolf and the agreement that was reached in Cavtat on that day?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there is no mention whatsoever.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was that a noteworthy event? In terms of its importance, wasn't it supposed to be included in this report?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour. I have to object unless the Defence is overlooking its paragraph 3 of the document it's putting in.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, under item 3, it says: "I decided to continue following the agreed cease-fire." At that time, even before the 5th of December, had there been a cease-fire that was in force?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I informed the commander of the 2nd Operational Group about the details and all points of the agreement. So whether it was before this or whether Zec, the chief of staff, had already sent the report I don't know. But the commander of the 2nd Operational Group was made aware of the details of that agreement, and that is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Not in dispute for who, Mr. Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not in dispute in terms of what I have been saying, whether the command of the 2nd Operational Group and the commander were made aware of the details of the agreement of the 5th of December. Because that is the point. That is the essence. Because there's no mention of it in the report as to whether the commander, my superior officer, was informed about this or not. As a matter of fact, we even discussed whether there should -- whether ships should be checked at sea or in the Port of Gruz.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, in the last sentence, the chief of staff, what does he inform the superior command of, last sentence in paragraph 4?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: That "morale is affected very adversely by ships exiting and entering the Port of Dubrovnik."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have the text yet again.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So tell me what is this? What kind of adverse affect is this on morale, and whose morale at that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Every week, two or three foreign ships would sail in to the Port of Dubrovnik, as well as Croatian ships, ships that were bringing in aid, food aid, medicine, and other supplies. There was an incident then between a ship called Cap d'Afrique, a French boat, which did not allow this check to be carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. Your Honour, I would like to ask for this document to be admitted into evidence as a Defence exhibit, and could it please be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: This exhibit is D61.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, in your interview in July 2002, that is pages 175 and 176 of that interview, I am going to read out the question that was read out to you. This is the English version that I'm talking about. This is what you were asked. The investigator asked you: "At what time did the meeting end, or rather these concrete negotiations on the 5th of December?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note that they do not have the text.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Answer. You say, "I know that it was lunchtime, meaning it could have been around 3.00. Around that. 1500 hours in the afternoon." The investigator asks you then yet again: "Will you tell us what you did on the 5th of December in the afternoon and in the evening? Who did you meet? How many meetings did you have and with who?" You answer the following: "I think -- I mean I do not remember the details, but I know that after the report I sent to the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, I issued an order to Chief of Staff Zec in relation to the cease-fire. From Cavtat, I went to Kumbor to my headquarters. Since this was completed successfully, I thought that there was no need for me to have any further meetings with my command. I spent the night at headquarters, too, and I resolved the question related to the evacuation of the units from the 5th Sector of Pula." That is page 175 of the English translation. And page 176, in response to a further question by the investigator: "Did you have a meeting in the afternoon with the chief of staff, or did you only talk to him? What did you tell us about that?" Your answer is as follows: "I think that I let him know about all of that over the telephone from the headquarters in Cavtat. Since the situation was stable, a cease-fire was concluded, we did not have any obligations why I would be duty-bound to give any kind of orders to the commanders." The investigator then asks: "Where did you phone him? Where was he then?" Answer: "He was certainly in Kupari at the forward command post." From this part of the interview that you gave to the investigators, it can be derived that it's not only that you did not go to Trebinje to see the commander of the operational group, that you did not go to Kupari, that you carried out all these conversations by and that you briefed everybody over the phone, too. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but I told you before that what the difference was between that interview in July which was before I had read and studied all the documents in the military archives. And this was before I talked to the senior members of the staff of my command who were then in Kupari. I think that as a matter of fact I said that there was a briefing on the 5th of December. I'm not sure. But I think that that is what I said somewhere and that that's what's written. However, that was not correct. There was no briefing on the 5th of December because I attended the negotiations. And the chief of staff postponed that briefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, tell me, is there any written evidence in any single document that on that date, the 5th of December, you were in Trebinje and that you were in Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that in addition to the war logbook, there are witnesses who are alive and who told me that I came to Kupari from the direction of Trebinje. That is Admiral Zec, Frigate Captain Kozaric, Colonel Kovacevic. All three of them were at the command post in Kupari. All three confirmed what I said to you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, when did Admiral Zec confirm to you what you told us here today? I'm interested in the time frame.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We discussed that not only when the indictment was issued, but a lot before that, when I as a retired person came to his command to look for documents and to talk to him about these events that took place during that war and that operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you got this information from Zec and verified it with him before 2001, since you've been retired since 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps not only this particular piece of information, but regarding all these events we discussed them then. I asked him also before the indictment was issued. I also asked him where the war logbook was. Then, the directive.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please, Mr. Jokic, answer my concrete question. The documents are not the issue now. But this fact that has to do with your stay in Cavtat and your travelling on that day. You say that among others, you confirmed this through your conversation with Admiral Zec. I'm asking you before -- whether this took place before this indictment was issued, and it was issued, if I'm not mistaken, in October 2001. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was before I went to The Hague. I cannot give you the exact time. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. If that was before you went to The Hague that you checked out this fact, why, then, as regards the interview in July 2002, why did you not present that fact that way to the investigators, the way I read this paragraph out to you just now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Back then, I had not yet studied the files. I probably found something in the files later. I had not yet talked to Kozaric, who was the person most familiar with all of that. He had, after all, been the duty officer. It's only after I had managed to do all of that in the autumn of 2002, I believe, that I knew exactly what had happened on that day. To the best of my recollection, I can tell you why I have submitted that I had been in Trebinje on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: We've heard that before, but I was asking but the discrepancy between your statement and what you're telling us today. Do you remember at all this journey after the talks in Cavtat?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not remember. Back then, I said that I didn't remember that journey. However, members of my command reminded me of where I had been, where I had come from, which was Trebinje, and what I had ordered them personally. I myself, however, do not remember the journey. That much is correct. If I had remembered, I would have said so back in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There would not have been any reason for me to change anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: The intelligence organ of the command of the 9th VPS, on the 5th of December in the evening, despite the cease-fire that had been agreed, did they not receive word that ammunition supplies were running from Storn [phoen] towards Dubrovnik that evening? You as the commander, did you have this information?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember there were things like that. I'm not sure if on that particular day, but there were a number of times when this happened. From the direction of Storn.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know exactly what the situation of the unit was in the immediate blockade of the town on the 5th of December in the afternoon? If you could please just tell us briefly where each of the units were.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those units that were of importance in relation to the blockade of the town, the 4th Battalion of the 472nd Brigade, for example, were positioned at the Dubrava ridge. I could also enumerate the companies if you would like me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: There's no need to. Just briefly in a very general way.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The positions had not changed since the 12th of November. The 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade above Mokosica. Also Petrovo Selo, that position had not changed since the units entered Mokosica on the 21st of November. And the remaining units, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Do you know what the situation was in the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade and the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Partisan Motorised Brigade on the evening of the 5th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure what you mean about "the situation." The units report according to the schedule by phone. If there is nothing special to report, then the commanders report by telephone. They usually say "the situation is regular, this or that happened" and then the operations duty officer gathers all this information and sends it on to the command of the 2nd Operational Group. On that particular evening, I had not received word of anything special happening in those units.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: If anything special or out of the ordinary had happened, would that have been recorded anywhere? Would you have been informed as well as your superior command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that would have been the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Did you take any special measures in relation to the order by the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, his order in relation to the cease-fire that was imminent and that was to take effect on the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I reckoned that at the moment that in addition to this order regarding the cease-fire, there was no need to take any other measures because the cease-fire had been in force for quite some time, and there were no combat operations with the possible exception of minor acts of provocation, sporadic ones. I reckoned that this was not a situation where any other special measures were to be taken in order to ensure that the cease-fire ordered by the commander of the 2nd Operational Group was observed.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In view of the intelligence that you had and the reports you received from your units around Dubrovnik, the reference is above all to the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade, and bearing in mind the importance of the agreement that was to be signed on the 6th of December, didn't this, despite everything, require particular attention to be paid to those units and perhaps the sending of people from the command to be there with the soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know why I would have done anything like that. In between the 13th of November and the 5th of December, as regards that particular battalion, we had no situations where a group of soldiers launched an attack, let alone any major units. The only thing that did occur were minor acts of provocation on both sides. But there were no other incidents, no other instances where this unit was disobedient, that their morale was that low, or any indication of any serious intention to violate the cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Tell me, the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade, did they report about the situation along the line of separation on the 5th of December in the evening? Did they report about the situation to their superior command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. There were duty-bound to report on everything that was out of the ordinary. If there was anything out of the ordinary or any acts of provocation, they would have been duty-bound to report that. I do not know that they actually did on the 5th, on the evening of the 5th. If there was anything like, probably those were minor things. But I'm not aware of any.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether the commander of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade on the evening of the 5th of December reported to the command of the 9th VPS that fire had been opened on the positions of his battalion that same evening?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know if any such information ever reached the operation centre of the 9th VPS at all?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not for as long as I was at the command post. I was not informed about anything like that at the operations centre in Kumbor either. If there had been anything like that, it could only have been of that nature. And therefore, I was not to be informed at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What about if the commander of the 3rd Battalion on the 5th of December at five minutes to midnight got in touch to say that his battalion had come under fire, would you have been informed about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They wouldn't report to me. If that had been the case, if there had been the odd volley or some rifle fire, that was a frequent occurrence. But I do not know that anything like that happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you perhaps know on the 5th of December or later if the commander of the 3rd Battalion on that same evening of the 5th of December, at 23.55 hours asked for a protest to be filed with the Croatian side because his lines had come under fire?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of anything like that. I probably would have learned the next morning or during the night. There would be someone to wake me up and inform me. The operations duty officer would have informed me because this would have constituted sufficient reason for me to be informed. This didn't happen, and I do not know that there is any written proof of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: You do not know if he requested instructions from the command of the 9th VPS with regard to this situation along their line of separation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When precisely?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: On the 5th of December at 23.55 hours.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The first information I received was at 04.55. That was the morning of the 6th.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know if the command of the 9th VPS approved the request of the commander of the 3rd Battalion to file a protest note with the Croatian side that same evening?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. The evidence is he didn't even know about a protest note.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Well, I think he has asked if he knows, and the answer would obviously be no. Is that so, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is the very first I hear of this, of any protest note ever being filed. And I don't know who by or who would have been behind it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you then tell me who was at the operations centre of the 9th VPS on the 5th of December in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At Kupari or at Kumbor? Because there were two operations centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Forward command post of Kupari.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Captain Kozaric was there, as well as the operations duty officer, Mitar Dzelebdzic. There was supposed to be another officer there to relieve those two, but that was a low-ranking officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: In your talks with Kozaric before you arrived in The Hague and after your arrival in The Hague and went back home in 2001 until 2003, did he ever mention to you any information like this in relation to the evening of the 5th of December, anything to do with reporting by the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he didn't mention that. The only thing he mentioned was the succession of those events begins when he woke me up at 04.45, woke me up to tell me about that. And after that. But up to that point, nobody had informed me, nor do I know that he ever referred to any protest notes or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: What was the last time you spoke to your command on the 5th of December, to the forward command post at Kupari?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what the last time was. When I left Kupari, I had to be in Kumbor by 1900 hours. That's for sure. But I do not remember any conversation. There was no need for that, nor did anyone inform me about anything out of the ordinary happening in relation to the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. When you say that there were three officers at the operations centre, can you tell me about this duty. How long does one stay on duty and how frequently do they take turns between midnight and 8.00 in the morning, for example? I do not expect a single officer to be manning the desk for 24 hours in a row.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There are three shifts. Depending on what's going on and depending on the need, those three shifts can become two shifts. There's always one officer that's always awake. There's another officer who is preparing to take over, and the third officer is resting. That's how it works at the operations centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: This taking of turns, is it usually done in the evening?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The shifts are between 8.00 and 12.00, the first one. The next one is between 12.00 and 4.00 in the morning. And the third shift is between 4.00 in the morning and 8.00 in the morning. Three shifts.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: So which is the shift after midnight? I want to know about the -- about nighttime. Which one would that be?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second shift is between 12 -- between midnight and 4.00 in the morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know perhaps who specifically was on duty that particular night between midnight and 4.00 in the morning?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I talked to the chief of the operations department, Kozaric, who had at his disposal another two officers. I did not talk to those two officers, so I can't tell you exactly if you want to go further into the details. Mitar Dzelebdzic was on duty between midnight and 4.00 in the morning. I know that Kozaric was also awake, and that he was familiar with everything that went on during that night or that day, the 6th of December.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you by any chance remember the name of the third officer who was there?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I can't remember his name. I really can't. He was a lower ranking officer, a captain, perhaps, a major. But I can't tell you who it was specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: And tell me this, please: Were you informed that during the night, that is to say, from midnight until 5.00 a.m. On the 6th of December 1991, that fire was opened from the positions of the Croatian side targeting the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade, and that the operations centre was informed about that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I was woken up at 4.55, and I can give you the time not on the basis of my memory but what the secretary and Kozaric said. They said that I had been woken up at 4.55, and Frigate Captain Kozaric then proceeded to inform me that he had heard explosions of shells and that there was firing in the area of Zarkovica, Dubac, and Srdj. But that was half an hour before that. He said he had heard this half an hour prior to me being woken up. And then he called up the 3rd Battalion at Brgat, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now what I'm interested in is this: Your awareness of having been woken up at 4.55 a.m. and being given this information, do you remember that happening? Or did Kozaric tell you about it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I don't remember the time, the exact hour. But in the war logbook, I found this entry, and he had recorded it in the logbook. But yes, he told me. He said that it was exactly at that time. And all the remaining time entries are -- were entered by him and his command. I don't remember the times exactly myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right, thank you. Now, do you know why during the night no steps were taken, no measures were taken with respect to the fact that the positions of the 3rd Battalion had been targeted?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. That is not what the evidence has ever been. If you go back in the record, it's -- there are reports. But this is simply an incorrect assertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on page 54, line 6, the witness spoke about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me anything?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ... Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, what the evidence has been is there were reports of fire. From whom -- that was counsel testifying about the Croatians. It wasn't the witness saying that it happened. And the basis for this question is presupposing an origin of fire is a foregone conclusion. That's just not the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think your question has gone beyond the supporting evidence. If you take those bits out, you can still ask a useful question.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Yes. Perhaps I did misspeak.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: But do you know whether in the course of the night anything was undertaken with respect to opening -- with respect to the fact that fire had been opened? And this fact was conveyed to you at 4.55 in the morning by the duty officer Kozaric.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was undertaken, nor was I informed that there was firing and that measures had been taken except for the firing that we're talking about now at 4.45.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know when Captain Kozaric took up his duties at the operations centre on -- of the 9th VPS on the 6th of December? When did he come to work or take up his duties that day? At what time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was in the operations centre. There's a -- there are beds there. He doesn't go anywhere. He sleeps there. There are three of them. Perhaps one of them can go somewhere else, but two of them have to be on the spot. So he's not coming or going. He was there all the time. So everything that happens, if anything happened, he would be the chief, and he would have had to have been woken up, and if there was any firing he would have had to have been informed about it, even if he wasn't on duty himself, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, did Kozaric at 4.45 a.m. of the 6th of December inform you that Kovacevic had one dead soldier and two wounded soldiers, and that they were being heavily fired at from Srdj and Dubrovnik?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: When Kozaric told you that, did he wake you up at the command in Kumbor?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Is it right that faced with a situation of this kind, that is to say that when Kozaric informed you that Kovacevic was being fired at from Srdj and Dubrovnik, that you as the commander of the 9th military naval sector continued to sleep on?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There was no question of that, and that's what it says in the transcript. There would be absolutely no question of that. Heaven forbid, I was in the office, and my bed is in the office next to the operations centre in Kumbor. So how could I go on sleeping in that kind of situation? Heaven forbid. Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you say that after being informed at 4.45 a.m., you did not continue sleeping?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not continue sleeping, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I am now going to remind you of what you told the investigators in your interview between the 6th to the 12th of September [as interpreted] 2003 when asked that same question. And you'll find that on page 133 and 134 of the English translation of your interview. The investigator asks you the following: "Where were you on the morning of the 6th of December? When did you wake up?" And your answer: "At a quarter to 5.00. I have looked through my notes once again, and Kozaric's, too. And it says there at 4.45, Kozaric, from Kupari, on the IKM, woke me up and told me that Captain Kovacevic had just called him from Brgat and told him that he was coming under heavy mortar fire from Srdj, Nuncijata, and that he also had one dead man and two wounded soldiers. And he now says, Kovacevic says to Kozaric, I am now going from the command post at Brgat to Zarkovica to assess the situation. And that is 4.45 minutes. Is that -- that's what the investigator asks. And you confirm that, yes, that's right. And the investigator goes on to ask, "And you yourself were in Kumbor." Your answer was "Yes." The investigator: "Were you sleeping at the command in Kumbor or in your apartment?" And your answer was: "At the command, in my office there." And then on page 134, the investigator goes on to ask you: "So you were woken up before the attack began?" Answer: "Yes, yes, yes." Investigator: "The attack began at 4.45." Answer: Yes. At 5.00, no, I was saying what reports? The attack is something else. I was saying how I was informed about what was happening. But we'll come to that."

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have to ask that the witness be given a transcript because the translation that I have is not translated --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreters note that they do not have a copy of the original text.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I think it's only fair to present this to the witness in his own language to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am reading the official translation, which the Defence was provided, and I'm reading it in the B/C/S language, which Mr. Jokic understands, which Witness Jokic understands. So may I please be allowed to continue. I have two more paragraphs and passages to read out to the witness. I can give the witness a copy via the usher if need be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think that would help.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At the end of page 134 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: [Previous interpretation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I am, Your Honour. May I just read out two more lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: At the end of page 134 of the English translation in English, and 125 is the page for the B/C/S, you state as follows: "I say to Kozaric, I've monitored the situation, and if necessary, wake me up.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or words to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Kozaric woke me out at 6.00 again -- by -- over the phone via my aide de camp, and the aide de camp Ivan Hrvoje, I can't quite remember -- Ivan Hrvoje.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could I ask the usher to come and collect that document.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't have to show it to me. I remember it well.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, the quotation that I read out to you was from the interview you gave in September last year after you had pleaded guilty on the indictment. So up until then, you had conducted all these conversations and interviews with people from your staff that you mentioned here. Is it, then, correct that you continued sleeping after being informed first by Kozaric at 4.45 about the situation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true. Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me why you told the investigators that?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't say that I was sleeping. I just said that Kozaric called -- I said "call me, inform me." I didn't say I was sleeping. God forbid.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Was -- is the transcript erroneous?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably what my words were imprecisely recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, do you know that a videotape of your interview with the investigator also exists?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I suppose so.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have to object. I think there's confusion that's being -- it appears possibly being put forth on in an intentional manner on timing. The evidence in chief addresses the issue, and perhaps it would be more appropriate to refer back to the evidence in chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: You have lost me there, Ms. Somers. I'm not sure what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The evidence in chief -- sorry, I'm trying to remember myself. I don't have the transcript. But I recall that it was mentioned, that he was awakened at a certain hour, at 4.45, and then certain things happened. This is not what is being presented to this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The witness has said today that he was wakened at 4.45 and that he did not go back to sleep. A passage is being put to him from his interview in December which on its face suggests that he was woken again sometime around 6.00. I think that's the simple issue. And he says of that, well, if that's what's recorded of what I said, it is wrongly recorded or perhaps I spoke loosely. I didn't go back to sleep. Have I understood your evidence correctly, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely correct, Your Honour. That's just how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that you didn't tell the investigators that you slept after that first call?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, how could any commander continue to sleep after everything that he had heard? What are you on about?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the usher to hand the tab back to me, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, just to make the record clear, that the evidence earlier is that after the second call, he did not go to sleep -- I think, again, the level of back and forth, and I'll certainly try to clean it up on redirect. But I must say this is taking the evidence in chief and not presenting it to the witness as it was presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I don't think that was necessary at this point. The question was based firmly on the admiral's evidence of a few minutes ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection now because the way I read it out, the transcript of this interview, the witness confirmed that it was correct. And indubitably, he did have the transcript in front of him. And now my colleague is saying that I tried to distort what it says in the transcript and present it in a different light. That really is going too far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we can put aside the to and fro between counsel. I think the Chamber is well aware of the evidence of the admiral on the point and of the apparent difference between what he now says and what was said in the earlier interview. So we can move on from there. I'm particularly concerned now to delay you because of the hour, Mr. Rodic.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you, Your Honour, I'll do my best.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, why did you not immediately at 4.45 send your officers out to see what the situation was if you knew already how close your units were to the town of Dubrovnik and how strong their artillery was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Why would I do that if the commander of the battalion did not report to me, as commander, and why he was evading the telephone all together so that he would not speak to me? At that time, I thought there was no need to intervene and to send any officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, tell me, in the period from 4.45, when Kozaric woke you up, until his second call to you, at about 6.00 that morning of the 6th of December, can you tell me what you specifically did within that time span?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't know, Mr. Rodic, what I did. Probably, since I had already been awakened, I had to get dressed or go and take a shave or something like that, or perhaps I had other physiological needs. I cannot say exactly what I did then 13 years ago after having been awakened. Of what relevance is that for this, for the nature of the examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do beg your pardon for having to go back to this. But with the assistance of my colleague, I received the information that we were dealing with. On the sixth cassette, or rather the sixth CD from March 2004, Mr. Jokic in response to the investigator's question says: At 6.15 when he was awakened again, Kozaric told him that Kovacevic had called him and informed him that the fire was so unbearable that there is one dead man and two wounded, and that he was leaving Brgat to go to Zarkovica to see what this was all about. Was Mr. Jokic giving the wrong answers to the investigator's questions then?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are you asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see that this partly coincides with that and partly does not because the questions are such that a person cannot repeat the identical answer to thousands of questions. The report of Captain Kovacevic stating that he had one dead man and two men wounded. As you quoted the transcript a while ago, you said that it was at 4.45. And now it's 6.15. Do you see the difference?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: I understand that. But the only place where there is no discrepancy is: In both cases, you say that you were awakened yet again at 6.00. There is no discrepancy is there. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am telling you that I did not sleep. Now, you can quote whatever you want.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: All right. One dead soldier and two wounded soldiers at 4.45 in the morning on the 6th of December, is that a serious loss for the 3rd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Objection, Your Honour. Mr. Rodic just indicated that at the proofing session he is talking about notified at 6.00 something about the alleged facilities and lethal or whatever the term was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The admiral's evidence here put it at 4.45. This earlier statement in March of this year put it at 6.15. Mr. Rodic may or may not want to clarify that difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Mr. Jokic, did you say that at 4.45, Kozaric informed you that Captain Kovacevic has one man dead and two men wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wanted to draw your attention to that a short while ago when comparing these two conversations at 4.45 and 6.00 and to say that it differs, and it was not possible to establish it correctly. I think that at 4.45 I was only informed that the battalion had been fired upon, but not that they had sustained any losses, and only at 6.00 I had been informed that there had been losses. Kozaric was not certain, and I was not certain most of all. However, since you were not interested in that, you were interested in whether I was asleep or not, I did not pursue that any further in terms of how the conversation evolved. That is why you now have in this transcript of March that I'm saying that at 10 past 6.00 or around 6.00 that I had received information that he had one man dead and two men wounded. I think that that is the most accurate of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Do you know when exactly you received information that the 3rd Battalion had one man dead and two men wounded?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm saying that I'm not sure. I think it was at 6.00, not at 4.45. But if you wish to know the actual truth, we're only discussing transcripts, but the actual truth is that he did not have any losses either at 4.45 or at 6.00. That's the real truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Now I don't understand anything.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: Please, you're answering my questions. Several times you stated that you had been informed about the losses of the 3rd Battalion, under oath. While giving evidence now, here, before the Honourable Trial Chamber, and also during the previous interviews. Now, it no longer matters whether it was at 4.45 or at 6.00. But as information that you had received, this is something that you stated under oath during the examination-in-chief and during the cross-examination. Now, you are claiming that what you had said is not true. Can you explain that now?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Sorry, that is simply not what has been said. I know the Chamber will discern, but it is so misleading. It is relaying of information which is not even verified that is the subject of whatever discussion would have been with the operations officer. That is simply not what the admiral has said. And I just would ask that counsel conduct his questioning according to what the evidence has been.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think, Mr. Rodic, the problem is that you are taking as fact what may or may not have been reported. The report may have been given; it need not be accurate. But I don't think it can be said the admiral said that he knew as a fact that there was one dead and two wounded. He had reports of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that with this type of objections, my learned friend is testifying instead of Witness Jokic, and then Witness Jokic repeats her statements made while objecting. My question was simple and clear. Several times before this Honourable Trial Chamber, the witness stated that he had been informed, that he had received information in the morning, the exact time is not important now, about one dead and two wounded from the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And I asked him what he did on the basis of this information, not what he established in 2002 or in 2003 and so on when he was carrying out his investigation. I'm asking him about what happened in 1991.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is the point that you put to the witness that something he said was not true, was that directed to his statement that he had been informed about the casualties, or was it directed to saying that there were no casualties in truth, whatever had been reported to him?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm asking him what happened in 1991, what he knew then, what he did on the basis of that information, or rather on that morning of the 6th of December. That is what the witness talked about here previously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: I think we are at cross-purposes, and both Ms. Somers and I understood your question one way, and you may have intended it another. Can we ask the admiral: Were you informed by your staff on the morning of the 6th of December that the battalion had suffered one dead and two wounded?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are you able to be sure whether that was at 0445 hours or 0615 hours or thereabouts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think it was at the later hour. During the first reporting, the only information given was that the other side was firing with their artillery. However, there were not only these two conversations, only two conversations were referred to here. But of course, there were several conversations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Are they conversations that you had or conversations between the unit in the field and your staff?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, between myself and this Frigate Captain Kozaric, the duty officer at the centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Have we cleared up something for you there, Mr. Rodic? The greater question is that we have --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In part, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: -- come to time. Are you as good as finished, or what is your situation?

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm not, Your Honour. I kindly ask you to understand me, you see, because of this abundance of material, we have other documents other important documents related to the 6th and 7th of December that the Defence needs to put into evidence. I kindly ask you that you understand our situation and please allow us to finish the cross-examination on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: There can be no prospect of that, Mr. Rodic. We made it clear two days ago that the cross-examination had to come to an end and that you should adjust your questions accordingly to what was most material. But there may be some hope for you. Ms. Somers, when we dealt with this matter, I was rash enough to think that one session would be enough for your re-examination. Is that the case?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: If Your Honour has in mind from this point or the break on, it would not. And I don't think it was rash, Your Honour. I think in all honesty I think you thought perhaps. But it has been a very detailed cross-examination. We would ask for more than one session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That gives you by the graciousness of Ms. Somers the rest of today, Mr. Rodic. We will allow you to continue for the final session today. And that will be it. So we will have a break now, and then continue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may, I would like to take this opportunity to address you briefly. Your Honour, by your leave, I would like to address you briefly. Very briefly indeed. Your Honours, the testimony of this witness, who is now before the Chamber, is probably one of the most important testimonies that the OTP intends to present before the Trial Chamber in relation to the guilt of the accused, General Strugar. The result of this testimony and the way in which this testimony takes place will be essential for your final decision in this legal matter. The fact that the Defence is limited in the scope of its cross-examination, I'm afraid may have fatal consequences as regards the first duty of everyone here in this courtroom, to ensure for a fair proceeding before this Trial Chamber in relation to the accused Pavle Strugar. I will try to give you the reasons now briefly. This witness ought to be shown a significant number of key documents, written evidence, that are crucial for this case, Your Honours. This witness should be presented with an entire set of written documents and other kinds of documents that also may have a significant bearing on your decision in this matter. The obligation to have a fair trial is included in what this witness should be shown and what should be presented before this Trial Chamber. With all due respect, Your Honours, and bearing the time constraints in mind, the constraints by both this Trial Chamber and the International Tribunal at large, we would like to reiterate our request for the Trial Chamber to reconsider its decision made two days ago and confirmed by a while ago. Can the Trial Chamber please kindly reconsider this decision and take into account all of our arguments in order to allow the Defence team to continue the cross-examination of this witness on Monday. We would really appreciate if this exception was made in this case. As for our part, and I believe we have offered ample demonstration of this, we shall do everything within our power so that all other testimonies and all other procedures before the final judgement can be expedited and reduced to the bare minimum, even to the detriment of our case if necessary. However, we would like our request to be reconsidered, and we would appreciate your decision being in favour of this request that we are making. It is with a great deal of regret, Your Honours, that we are requesting additional time on Monday. And if our request is not met, we would like to draw your attention to the fact that in order to have a fair trial, in order to assure that our client enjoys a fair trial, we shall unfortunately be compelled to lodge an appeal against such a decision on your part. It is with the deepest regret that I must say this, in view of the fact that the Trial Chamber has always treated the Defence team fairly and ensured that our client have a fair trial. Therefore, the Defence would like to ask for additional time to complete our cross-examination of Witness Jokic on Monday. Thank you very much, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Petrovic, you've said Monday. You've not said what time you would want on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for that, Your Honour. Your Honour, the Defence would like to ask for two further sessions on Monday, the first two, if possible. That would leave ample time to my learned friend and colleague to complete her re-examination. That would complete the examination of this witness on Monday, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: No, it wouldn't. That would leave Ms. Somers with only one session on Monday, and she has indicated she believes now, and I think on reasonable grounds, that she would need two sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, by your leave, in view of the importance of this whole issue, bearing in mind the time constraints, we are prepared to take up our further obligations as the Defence team to further reduce the time granted to us in relation to other witnesses. But we would very much appreciate being allowed to cross-examine this witness in the proper way, as I have defined before. You remember that at the last 65 ter Conference, we discussed the time constraints of this case, and we talked about a mere five weeks for the Defence case. I would like to use this opportunity to try to convince you that there is every indication and a lot of goodwill on the part of the Defence team for this not to even go on for a mere five weeks, but rather for a shorter time. May Your Honour take that into account, too, when making a final decision as to our request that was made before the break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: The Chamber would point out that the Prosecution's evidence in chief from the witness extended just beyond four days; that at the end of the day today, the cross-examination will have lasted virtually seven days. We had emphasised in the sittings here and in the 65 ter Conference recently the need for great attention to time, and therefore to concentrate questioning, and especially cross-examination, on matters that really were relevant. In the course of this cross-examination, it was two days ago that we very specifically indicated the duration of time that should be allowed. We had then thought that it would be possible to conclude the evidence of the present witness today. It is clear that the range of issues covered meant that we did not allow enough time for the Prosecution because we envisaged they would have only one session of re-examination.
